title: Keyhole (minimally invasive) bunion surgery vs open surgery: is it better?
seoTitle: Keyhole vs Open Bunion Surgery: What the Evidence Says
metaDescription: Minimally invasive (keyhole) vs open bunion surgery: how they differ, what studies show on pain, recovery and complications, and who may suit which approach.
intro: If you have already decided, with your surgeon, that a bunion needs surgery, the next question is often how it will be done. Many patients ask about "keyhole" or minimally invasive bunion surgery, which uses tiny cuts instead of one longer incision. This article explains how the two approaches differ, what the research actually shows, and where the evidence is still limited.
summary: Minimally invasive (keyhole) bunion surgery corrects the same bone deformity as open surgery, but through a few small cuts. Current evidence suggests results are broadly similar to open surgery, with possibly less pain in the early weeks. It is not proven to be better overall, long-term data is limited, and recovery still takes months either way.

sections.heading: What is minimally invasive (keyhole) bunion surgery?
sections.body: Minimally invasive bunion surgery, also called percutaneous surgery, straightens the big toe by cutting and shifting the bone through a few incisions of a few millimetres. The surgeon uses a small burr and live X-ray guidance instead of looking at the bone directly, then usually fixes the bone with screws. A bunion (hallux valgus) is not a lump that can simply be shaved off. The first metatarsal bone has drifted outwards and the big toe has angled inwards, so lasting correction usually means cutting the bone (an osteotomy) and realigning it. Both keyhole and open surgery do this; what differs is how the surgeon gets to the bone. If you are still deciding whether you need surgery at all, read Do I need bunion surgery? first.

sections.heading: How is it different from traditional open surgery?
sections.body:
Open surgery uses a single longer incision, usually along the inner side of the foot, so the surgeon can see the bone and cut it with a saw. Common open operations include the scarf and chevron osteotomies. Keyhole surgery reaches the same bone through tiny cuts, guided by X-ray images, without opening up the joint.

The table summarises the practical differences. Both approaches aim for the same result: a straighter toe, less pain and a foot that fits more comfortably in a shoe.

sections.heading: What does the evidence say about pain, recovery and complications?
sections.body:
Studies so far suggest keyhole surgery gives similar results to open surgery, with some showing less pain early on. Large reviews have not found a clear difference in complication rates. However, many studies are small or of mixed quality, so it is fair to say the evidence is encouraging but not yet conclusive.

A 2022 meta-analysis in Frontiers in Surgery (Ji and colleagues) pooled 22 studies covering 790 feet treated with keyhole surgery and 838 treated with open surgery. It reported less pain in the early phase after keyhole surgery, shorter operating and hospital times, and no significant difference in overall complication rate. Pain scores at final follow-up were not significantly different. The authors themselves noted high variation between studies and called for larger, better trials. One included study found longer X-ray time with keyhole surgery.

In the UK, NICE (June 2024) reviewed 11 sources of evidence and concluded that these techniques can be used as an option, that there are no major safety concerns, and that they appear to work about as well as open surgery. NICE also noted there is no evidence that the bone heals faster than with open surgery, and that longer-term recovery pain did not appear to differ.

sections.heading: Does a bunion come back more or less after keyhole surgery?
sections.body:
We do not yet have reliable long-term data showing that keyhole surgery reduces or increases the chance of a bunion coming back. Recurrence can happen after any bunion operation, and is influenced by the severity of the deformity, how well it was corrected, healing, and footwear afterwards.

The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) lists recurrence among the possible complications of bunion surgery in general, and says minimally invasive bunion surgery has not been widely accepted and needs more long-term research. NICE has asked surgeons in the UK to record every patient in a registry partly so that longer-term outcomes, including recurrence, can be tracked.

sections.heading: Who might suit keyhole surgery, and who might suit open surgery?
sections.body:
There is no single answer. The choice depends on the size and type of your deformity, whether the big toe joint is arthritic, bone quality, your other health conditions, and above all your surgeon's training and experience with each technique. A well-done open operation and a well-done keyhole operation can both give good results.

Points worth discussing with your surgeon:
bullets: How severe is my bunion, and is the big toe joint itself worn out (arthritis)? Some conditions need a different operation altogether.
Which technique do you use most often, and why do you recommend it for my foot?
Will screws be used, and might they need removing later? NICE advises that patients be told about the possibility of implant removal.
How much weight can I put on the foot afterwards, and for how long will I need a special shoe?

sections.heading: What is recovery like, and when can I wear normal shoes?
sections.body:
Recovery is measured in months, not days, whichever technique is used. A smaller scar does not mean the bone heals faster. According to AAOS, full recovery often takes up to 6 months, and some swelling commonly lasts 6 months to a year after bunion surgery.

AAOS also notes that the foot usually needs support from dressings or a brace for 6 to 12 weeks, and that where walking is allowed soon after surgery, a special surgical shoe is used to protect the correction. Driving may be restricted until the bones have healed. Your surgeon will give you a timeline specific to your operation.

On footwear, be realistic: AAOS cautions that bunion surgery may not allow you to wear narrow, pointed shoes or a smaller size, and that returning to that type of shoe can make the bunion come back. A roomy toe box is a lifelong friend. Bunion surgery should not be done for cosmetic reasons alone.

faqs.q: Is keyhole bunion surgery better than open surgery?
faqs.a: Not proven. Current studies, including a 2022 meta-analysis and NICE's 2024 review, suggest results are broadly similar, with possibly less pain in the early weeks after keyhole surgery. Long-term evidence is still limited.

faqs.q: Will I recover faster after minimally invasive bunion surgery?
faqs.a: You may have less pain early on, but NICE found no evidence that the bone heals faster than after open surgery. Full recovery after bunion surgery often takes up to 6 months, and swelling can last up to a year.

faqs.q: Is minimally invasive bunion surgery safe?
faqs.a: NICE concluded there are no major safety concerns, but said these are challenging techniques that should only be done by surgeons with specific training. Risks such as infection, stiffness, screw irritation or recurrence apply to any bunion operation.

faqs.q: Can the bunion come back after keyhole surgery?
faqs.a: Yes, recurrence is possible after any bunion surgery. There is not yet reliable long-term data to say whether it is more or less common after keyhole surgery. Wearing narrow, pointed shoes again can increase the risk.

faqs.q: Can I wear normal shoes after bunion surgery?
faqs.a: Eventually most people return to comfortable, roomy shoes. You will need a protective surgical shoe or support for several weeks first, and narrow or pointed shoes may not be suitable even after full recovery.
